newsitem.title: USA: Dollar pros on lookout for reversal in up trend.
newsitem.headline: Dollar pros on lookout for reversal in up trend.

text.p: The dollar's gradual ascent against European currencies from its March 1995 post-World War II lows may be peaking and analysts said they are searching for signs that the long-term trend has reversed.

"We have finally, after 22-months, reached target-bands in the dollar against European currencies that we expected in March 1995," said Darren Spain, technical foreign exchange analyst at Credit Suisse.
"For the long-term, we have been bullish and now we are looking for signs of confirmation to be bearish."
In the latest surge of an almost two-year rally, the U.S. currency hit a fresh 29-month peak of 1.5925 marks and a 31-month high of 1.3796 Swiss francs on Monday.

Dan Ascani, president and director of research at Global Market Strategists Inc, back in 1995 forecast dollar/mark would rebound to the 1.58 level from its record lows. He called last week's move through this level a warning light.

"Once the forecast resistance level has been hit, we then need to see confirmation that it is going to cause a turn. It is a bit too early to confirm, but we are expecting the dollar to end its year-and-ten-month rally here," Ascani said.
Some dealers said they have put their clients on so-called "reversal watch".
"From a long-term perspective, we are at levels where we suggest to clients they stay short the dollar, long European currency positions," said a trader at a European bank here.
International economists cited two predominant but conflicting theories which muddle projections of the dollar's future valuation against most European currencies.
But Reuter surveys show most pundits expect the dollar/mark rate to peak in the first quarter of 1997 and subsequently drop below 1.54 by year-end.

Analysts said the main threat to the greenback is an exacerbation of the present dollar overhang. If the U.S. trade deficit remains chronically high, as many predict, this oversupply of dollars will only worsen, they said.

But another theory that European currencies will need to depreciate to boost those economies struggling with downsizings and structurally high unemployment may dominate and buoy the U.S. unit, analysts said.

"There are strong arguments to be made in both cases, but ... I still say on balance the supply-demand situation of the dollar says it ultimately goes back down once again," said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc Corp.
"As a result, the European economies will grow more slowly than would otherwise be the case."
Rothfield forecast dollar/mark rising to 1.65 by March, but falling to between 1.40 and 1.50 marks within two years.

However, not all analysts foresee a halt to the dollar's climb. Randolph Donney, director of capital markets research at Pegasus Econometric Group, when asked about a near-term reversal, said: "No, I don't see that at all. But I do see the possibility of a substantial correction over the next couple of months."
He said the dollar's correction since March 1995 has been longer but of less magnitude than past major moves.

"If you look at the very long-term trend, you see a pattern of less and less progress with each successive attempt to move the dollar/mark lower on these long-term swings to downside. I see the very long-term momentum to the downside turning to the dollar's favor," Donney said.
